newsitem.title: USA: U.S. adults have negative view of teen-agers - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. adults have negative view of teen-agers - study.

text.p: Most adult Americans have negative views of teenagers and children and believe the country's youth face a moral crisis, according to a study published on Thursday.

Only 37 percent of adults believe today's children, once they become adults, will make the United States a better place, the study by the New York-based public policy research organisation Public Agenda said. It revealed high levels of antagonism toward teenagers and even young children.

Two-thirds of Americans used such adjectives as "rude," "irresponsible" and "wild," to describe teenagers, according to the report, "Kids These Days: What Americans Really Think About the Next Generation." Forty-eight percent said young children were "spoiled" and they were also characterised as "lacking discipline."

Another survey, conducted among 12- to 17-year-old Americans, revealed that the majority felt children their age needed more guidance from adults. Only 39 percent said it was very common to have parents who are good role models and teach their children right from wrong.
Most of the teens in the survey, 66 percent, said faith in God was an important part of their life. But few believed they were respectful toward each other or toward adults.

The two surveys were conducted by telephone interview within the continental United States last December. The first included 2,000 randomly selected adults plus 300 black parents and 300 Hispanic parents. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percent.

The researchers said they did the targeted interviews of black and Hispanic parents in order to compare their views with those of white parents. They found that all three groups were critical of teens and children.
The second survey interviewed 600 randomly selected people aged 12 to 17 years old. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent.

"Americans are frightened for -- and in some cases, frightened of -- our children, and fault parents for the problems they see," Public Agenda executive director Deborah Wadsworth said. "The public does acknowledge how difficult it is to be a parent in today's world but it is riveted by one goal -- the necessity of teaching all children the values of integrity, ethical behaviour, concern for others, respect, civility, compassion and responsibility."

More than 6 in 10 Americans believe young people failed to learn moral values such as honesty, responsibility and respect, the survey showed. Nine in 10 said the failure to learn values was widespread; only 8 percent said the problem was found mostly in children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

A majority also said they believe children thrive when their parents care for them and teach them right from wrong. They said the public looks to schools to supplement values taught by parents at home.
Respondents showed strong support for improving public schools, after-school programmes, volunteer organisations such as the Boy Scouts and tougher measures to keep children off the street.

"Americans rank government funding for child and health care programmes at the bottom of a list of 12 items that would be very effective in helping kids, in part because such programmes do not speak to their primary concerns about moral development," the report said.
The survey was conducted by Public Agenda for Ronald McDonald House Charities and The Advertising Council, organisations dedicated to improving the lives of children.
